article.overview: A near-infrared (NIR) spectrometer measures how strongly a surface reflects sunlight across a set of wavelengths in the near-infrared region. In this article the working band is roughly 0.7 to 2.6 µm; that band is a scope definition for this article, not a value published by any one instrument. Many minerals and water-bearing materials absorb light in characteristic places in this region, so a reflectance spectrum can help identify mineral groups. Scope of this entry: near-infrared spectrometers that record spectra from one ground footprint at a time, or along a narrow line, rather than as a two-dimensional image. Three flown examples are covered: the SMART-1 Infrared Spectrometer (SIR) on ESA's SMART-1 lunar mission, the Chandrayaan-1 Near Infrared Spectrometer (SIR-2) and the SELENE (Kaguya) Spectral Profiler (SP). The SP is included because two of its three channels (NIR1 and NIR2) lie in the near-infrared and its VIS channel covers only part of its range; its overlap with entry 062 should be checked when that entry is written. Out of scope and cross-referenced: imaging spectrometers that record a full spectrum for every pixel (entry 035, Hyperspectral imager); near-infrared framing cameras (entry 040, Near-infrared camera); short-wave infrared cameras (entry 041); thermal imagers (entry 036); visible and infrared spectrometers (entry 062, Visible and infrared spectrometer). Status summary: all three examples flew and were orbiter instruments. No lander-mounted point spectrometer, proposed concept or prototype is verified in the sources accessed, so none is described as flown or operating.
article.description: A near-infrared spectrometer splits incoming light into its wavelengths and records how much light falls in each one. The reflected sunlight from a surface has dips, called absorption features, at wavelengths that depend on the materials present. A spectrum with enough wavelength samples can show where those dips are, and scientists compare them with laboratory spectra of known minerals. The examples differ in how they look at the surface. The SMART-1 SIR and the Chandrayaan-1 SIR-2 each measure one ground footprint at a time, a spot about 0.2 to 2.5 km across depending on instrument and orbit. The SELENE SP observes a strip under the spacecraft, which it samples line by line as the spacecraft moves. The instruments share the same basic physics but differ in optics, wavelength range, sampling and status, so their numbers should not be compared as if they described one product.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The stated purposes differ between the examples. Lunar surface mineralogy: the MPS SIR-2 page describes the instrument as a redesigned, compact, monolithic grating near-infrared spectrometer [ref 4]; the ISRO page lists five objectives, including analysis of the lunar surface in geological and mineralogical units and the study of space weathering [ref 6]. Mineral mapping with a line-profiling spectrometer: the SP is described as separating reflected light into 296 wavelengths and observing the surface below the spacecraft [ref 7]. Secondary search summaries describe goals of mapping rock type and mineral abundance; these were not confirmed against a primary mission paper in this run [ref 8]. Spacecraft-borne point spectroscopy: the SMART-1 SIR was carried on the ESA SMART-1 spacecraft [ref 1, ref 2], and the MPS project page describes its detector cooling and footprint [ref 3]. The MPS SIR-2 page describes the later instrument as a redesign of the SIR flown on SMART-1 [ref 4].
article.operating_principle: The basic chain is the same in all three examples. Light is collected by a telescope or aperture, carried to a spectrometer, dispersed by a grating so that each wavelength falls on a different detector element, and recorded as a number for each wavelength. The MPS SIR-2 page states that light reaches the instrument through a fibre, and its schematic shows a fibre link between the optical box and the spectrometer body with a grating in the body [ref 4]. The SIR and SIR-2 detectors are arrays of 256 pixels, each a photodiode that converts incoming light into an electrical signal [ref 3, ref 4]. The SP uses a different arrangement: its optics pass reflected light to two gratings that spread it into 296 wavelengths, assigned to three spectral channels, VIS, NIR1 and NIR2 [ref 7, ref 8]. The SP principle diagram shows the instrument viewing a strip of surface about 500 m wide below a spacecraft at 100 km altitude [ref 7].
article.scientific_importance: Near-infrared spectra add information that a visible-light image cannot always provide. Absorption features from many silicate minerals, and from hydrated or water-related materials, lie in or near this band, so a spectrometer with well-calibrated near-infrared channels can support mineral identification across a region. The value of a particular instrument depends on its wavelength coverage, sampling, signal-to-noise ratio, calibration and spatial footprint, and these differ between the examples. The SIR-2 objectives listed by ISRO associate the instrument with lunar mineralogy and space weathering [ref 6]. The SP calibration paper (Yamamoto, 2011) is listed on the DARTS dataset page as the calibration reference [ref 8, ref 9]; it was not read in full in this run.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a near-infrared spectrometer. The three examples use different wavelength coverage, detectors, optics and mission platforms, and the sources accessed publish different sets of values. Where a source does not publish a value, this article says 'not publicly specified'. Each number is tied to the named instrument and to its source. Where sources disagree, both values are recorded; pre-launch and in-flight values are kept separate. The comparison table below lists values that the sources state; the columns are not directly comparable designs and the table is not a ranking.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: The SMART-1 SIR and Chandrayaan-1 SIR-2 are compact spectrometer units; the SIR-2 instrument unit is 260 mm x 171 mm x 143 mm per ISRO [ref 6]. The SP dimensions are not publicly specified in the sources accessed. Dimensions are not inferred for the SMART-1 SIR or the SP. The SIR-2 footprint of about 220 m and the SP swath of 500 m are geometric consequences of the instrument's viewing geometry and orbit altitude, not instrument dimensions [ref 4, ref 7].
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: The ESA pre-launch table gives 2.3 kg for SIR [ref 1]. ISRO gives 3.3 kg for SIR-2 [ref 6]. A design-phase value of 1.7 kg for SIR was reported in a search summary and not verified [ref 10]. Mass for the SP is not publicly specified in the sources accessed. Spacecraft masses in the sources are not instrument masses and are not used.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: ESA's pre-launch table gives 4.1 W for SIR [ref 1]. A design-phase value of 2.5 W was reported in a search summary and not verified [ref 10]. Power for SIR-2 and SP is not publicly specified in the sources accessed. No power value is inferred.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: All three examples operated, or were designed to operate, in the vacuum and thermal environment of the Moon. The sources accessed give no qualification, radiation or temperature-tolerance values for the SMART-1 SIR, Chandrayaan-1 SIR-2 or SELENE SP, so none is stated. Published operational facts: the SIR detector is cooled, and the MPS page says thermal background strongly affects measurements at higher temperatures [ref 3]. The SIR-2 optics include a fibre link between the optical head and the spectrometer body [ref 4]. The SP observes along a line under the spacecraft at 100 km altitude with a 500 m swath [ref 7]. The DARTS SP dataset is a processed, preliminary product [ref 8]. Reflectance spectroscopy depends on sunlight, so spectra depend on solar illumination and viewing geometry; the sources accessed do not quantify this for the three examples. This is a general physical constraint, not a value taken from one source.
article.limitations: The three examples are not interchangeable. Their wavelength ranges, sampling, footprints, platforms and dates differ, and a single table must not be read as a comparison of performance. Mass and power are not publicly specified for several instruments. Where values exist, they come from pre-launch documents or ISRO statements, and the SMART-1 values conflict. SIR-2 in-orbit performance and operating period are not confirmed in the sources accessed. The SP Yamamoto (2011) calibration paper was cited but not read in full, and the SP science goals rest partly on search summaries rather than primary mission papers. The DARTS SP dataset is preliminary and its processed subset covers a small south polar region rather than the whole Moon [ref 8].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: All three examples are orbiter payloads. None was delivered to the surface in the sources accessed, and none is described as deployed. The payload is integrated into a spacecraft on Earth, launched, transferred to the Moon, inserted into lunar orbit and commissioned. For an orbiter spectrometer the relevant interfaces are mounting and alignment to the spacecraft's pointing frame, detector cooling, power and data handling, and the altitude that sets footprint size [ref 3, ref 4, ref 7].
transportation_process: Integrate the spectrometer into the spacecraft on Earth, including alignment and mounting so that the look direction is known.

Launch the spacecraft and transfer to the Moon. The ESA pre-launch article describes a 15-18 month cruise phase before SMART-1 arrived at the Moon [ref 1]. The SMART-1 launch date was not verified in this run.
Insert the spacecraft into lunar orbit. The SP operated from about 100 km altitude [ref 7]. The SMART-1 lunar-orbit insertion date and the SIR-2 orbit were not verified in this run.
Commission and operate the instrument, including detector cooling and calibration. The MPS SIR page describes the need for cooling [ref 3].
Build the spectral data line by line or footprint by footprint along the orbit [ref 7, ref 8].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: The SMART-1 SIR, Chandrayaan-1 SIR-2 and SELENE SP were fixed to their host spacecraft. None is described as deployed or as having a separate deployment mechanism in the sources accessed.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: SMART-1 SIR on the ESA SMART-1 lunar mission [ref 1, ref 2, ref 3]; SIR-2 on Chandrayaan-1 [ref 4, ref 5, ref 6]; SP on SELENE (Kaguya) [ref 7, ref 8].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a specific lander, rover or other spacecraft is asserted beyond the host relationships stated in the sources. A new near-infrared spectrometer on a different spacecraft would need verified mass, power, dimensions, pointing and data interface documents for that vehicle. Several of those values are not publicly specified for these instruments.

article.historical_significance: The three examples come from separate programmes. SMART-1 flew an ESA lunar mission that ended with the spacecraft impacting the lunar surface in 2006 [ref 2]. The MPS page describes SIR-2 as a redesign of the SIR flown on SMART-1 [ref 4]. SELENE (Kaguya) carried the SP as part of the LISM suite [ref 7]. The DARTS dataset is the public archive of SP observations, although it is preliminary [ref 8]. This article does not rank the programmes or claim firsts that the sources do not state.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: SMART-1 SIR mass and power: the ESA pre-launch table gives 2.3 kg and 4.1 W [ref 1]; a design-phase paper reported 1.7 kg, 2.5 W, 256 channels and a 1 mrad field of view [ref 10]. That paper was not accessed, so the conflict is recorded and not resolved. SMART-1 SIR launch and lunar-orbit insertion dates were not verified; the end-of-mission date of 3 September 2006 is verified from the ESA fact sheet [ref 2]. SIR-2 in-orbit performance, data return and operating dates were not verified. SIR-2 power is not publicly specified; the ISSDC Chandrayaan-1 payload document was retrieved but not readable as text in this run, so its SIR-2 section was not used. SIR-2 wavelength range differs slightly between MPS (0.9-2.4 µm) and ISRO (0.93-2.4 µm) [ref 4, ref 6]; both are recorded. SP field of view and footprint values come from the LISM page, which does not state the altitude basis for the 562 x 400 m value [ref 7]. SP detector technology is not stated on the LISM page. SP science goals are from search summaries, not a primary mission paper accessed in this run [ref 8]. SP band counts differ (296 wavelengths on the LISM page against 181 bands in the DARTS processed subset) and are not reconciled. General statements about mineral absorption features are background knowledge and are not tied to a specific source. Images: reuse conditions were not checked and no full-resolution downloads were made. Four images were checked for HTTP 200 and visually inspected. No SMART-1 SIR hardware image was verified, so none is shown. Cross-references: imaging spectrometers are covered in entry 035, NIR framing cameras in entry 040, visible and infrared spectrometers in entry 062, and short-wave infrared cameras in entry 041. Sources consulted but not accessed in full: the Springer SMART-1 design paper (DOI 10.1023/A:1017065326516) and the Springer Kaguya overview paper (DOI 10.1186/BF03352789) redirected to a login page and were not read.

Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery.

data_quality_notes: SMART-1 SIR mass and power conflict: ESA pre-launch table (March 2003) gives 2.3 kg and 4.1 W [ref 1]; a design-phase paper reported 1.7 kg and 2.5 W, 256 channels and 1 mrad FOV [ref 10], taken from a search summary and not verified against the paper. Recorded, not resolved.
SMART-1 SIR launch date and lunar-orbit insertion date not verified in this run. End-of-mission date 3 September 2006 is verified from the ESA fact sheet [ref 2].

SMART-1 SIR opening angle and spectral resolution are not stated on the primary MPS page; the 6 nm per-pixel sampling is a calculation from 256 pixels across 0.9-2.4 µm, not a published resolution [ref 3].
SMART-1 SIR cooling temperature 'around -50 degrees' is given on the MPS page without a unit; the unit is not assumed in the article.
SIR-2 in-orbit performance, data return and operating dates are not verified; MPS pages give no operation dates or status [ref 4, ref 5].
SIR-2 power and opening angle are not publicly specified in the sources accessed. SIR-2 mass of 3.3 kg and dimensions of 260 x 171 x 143 mm come from the ISRO page only [ref 6].
SIR-2 wavelength range: MPS gives 0.9-2.4 µm [ref 4, ref 5]; ISRO gives 0.93-2.4 µm [ref 6]. Both are recorded.
SIR-2 semiconductor detector material not confirmed on a primary page; an InGaAs description from a search summary is not used.

SELENE SP field of view (0.23 deg) and spatial resolution (562 x 400 m) come from the JAXA LISM page, which does not state the altitude basis for the spatial value; the principle diagram shows a 500 m swath at 100 km altitude [ref 7].
SELENE SP band counts differ: 296 wavelengths on the LISM page [ref 7] against 181 bands in the DARTS processed subset (84 VIS, 97 NIR1) [ref 8]. These are different measures and are not reconciled.
SELENE SP mass, power and dimensions are not publicly specified in the sources accessed. SP detector technology is not stated on the LISM page.
SELENE SP science goals (rock type and mineral abundance) come from secondary search summaries, not from a primary mission paper accessed in this run [ref 8].

Yamamoto (2011) SP calibration paper [ref 9] was cited by the DARTS page but not read in full. The DARTS SP dataset is preliminary and its processed subset covers a small south polar region rather than the whole Moon [ref 8].
Springer design-phase SMART-1 paper [ref 10] and Springer Kaguya overview paper (DOI 10.1186/BF03352789) redirected to a login page and were not accessed.
ISSDC Chandrayaan-1 payload PDF (https://www.issdc.gov.in/docs/ch1/chandrayaan1_payload.pdf) was retrieved, but its compressed content was not readable as text in this run; no value is taken from it.
General statements about mineral absorption features in the 1-2.5 µm region are background knowledge not tied to a specific source.

Image reuse and rights conditions were not checked for the four article images. No full-resolution downloads were made. No SMART-1 SIR hardware image was verified, so the SMART-1 example has no images.

Cross-references: imaging spectrometers are covered in entry 035, NIR framing cameras in entry 040, visible and infrared spectrometers in entry 062 (overlap with the SP's VIS channel to be checked), and short-wave infrared cameras in entry 041.
